subject: pharmacology
title: Acetylcholine Synthesis, Storage, Release, and Cholinomimetic Agonists

steps.tx: Neurotransmission in the parasympathetic nervous system and somatic motor endplate relies on active **acetylcholine synthesis**. Extracellular choline is transported into the presynaptic nerve terminal by a high-affinity, sodium-dependent carrier mechanism. Once inside the terminal cytoplasm, choline combines with acetyl coenzyme A derived from mitochondrial pyruvate oxidation, establishing the primary neurotransmitter responsible for muscarinic and nicotinic signaling across synapses.
steps.say: Choline uptake by sodium-dependent transporters forms the rate-limiting step in acetylcholine synthesis.

steps.tx: The enzymatic esterification of choline and acetyl coenzyme A is catalyzed specifically by cytosolic **choline acetyltransferase**. This constitutive enzyme operates in cholinergic neuron terminals, rapidly transferring the acetyl moiety to yield acetylcholine. Newly formed acetylcholine is subsequently pumped into synaptic storage vesicles by a proton-antiporter vesicular acetylcholine transporter, where it is concentrated alongside adenosine triphosphate and proteoglycans awaiting calcium-triggered exocytosis.
steps.say: Choline acetyltransferase converts choline and acetyl-CoA into acetylcholine in presynaptic terminals.

right.title: Acetylcholinesterase
points: Hydrolyzes acetylcholine into acetate and choline
Target of reversible and irreversible inhibitors

steps.tx: Experimental pharmacologic blockade of presynaptic choline uptake is achieved with the research tool **hemicholinium**. By competitively inhibiting the high-affinity sodium-dependent choline transporter at the axolemma, hemicholinium depletes presynaptic acetylcholine reserves and abolishes cholinergic neurotransmission. A distinct blocker, vesamicol, selectively inhibits the vesicular acetylcholine transporter, preventing storage of synthesized neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles.
steps.say: Hemicholinium blocks axonal choline uptake while vesamicol prevents vesicular packaging.

rows: Depletes intracellular choline and ACh synthesis
Prevents vesicular ACh storage and packaging

steps.tx: Cholinergic actions on visceral target organs are mediated primarily by five distinct **muscarinic receptors M1 M2 M3**. M1 receptors reside in gastric parietal cells and cerebral cortex, signaling via Gq proteins and inositol trisphosphate. M2 receptors predominate in nodal cardiac myocardium, coupling to Gi proteins to slow heart rate. M3 receptors govern exocrine gland secretion, smooth muscle contraction, and endothelial nitric oxide release.
steps.say: Muscarinic M1, M2, and M3 receptors mediate parasympathetic effects through Gq and Gi protein signaling.

steps.tx: Rapid neurotransmission across autonomic ganglia and neuromuscular junctions is controlled by ligand-gated ionotropic **nicotinic receptors**. These pentameric ion channels consist of neuronal subtypes in autonomic ganglia and adrenal medulla, and muscular subtypes at skeletal motor endplates. Agonist binding opens central sodium channels, causing swift membrane depolarization, action potential propagation, and immediate contraction of voluntary striated skeletal muscle.
steps.say: Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated cation channels mediating rapid ganglionic and neuromuscular excitation.

steps.tx: Selective stimulation of urinary and gastrointestinal tract motility without substantial cardiac deceleration is achieved with **bethanechol**. Because of its carbamic ester substitution and beta-methyl carbon side chain, bethanechol resists degradation by acetylcholinesterase and pseudocholinesterase. Clinicians administer bethanechol orally or subcutaneously to alleviate non-obstructive postoperative urinary retention, neurogenic bladder atony, and congenital megacolon.
steps.say: Bethanechol selectively stimulates urinary bladder detrusor muscle while resisting cholinesterase breakdown.

steps.tx: This small amber bottle delivers one of the oldest cholinergic drugs still in daily eye practice. **Pilocarpine nitrate** two percent drops contract the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle, producing miosis and opening aqueous outflow pathways. The amber glass protects the solution from light, and the fine dispensing tip matters because a single controlled drop gives the intended effect without systemic cholinergic spillover.
steps.say: Pilocarpine two percent drops constrict the pupil and improve aqueous outflow. The amber bottle protects the solution, and the fine tip delivers one controlled drop.

steps.tx: Watch what one drop does in the first minutes after it lands. Muscarinic stimulation by **pilocarpine** pulls the iris sphincter tight, shrinking the pupil, and contracts the ciliary muscle so aqueous humour drains more freely through the trabecular meshwork. That paired action explains its place in angle closure management, where a smaller pupil and better outflow relieve the pressure surge together.
steps.say: One pilocarpine drop constricts the pupil and contracts the ciliary muscle, improving aqueous drainage. That paired action helps relieve an angle closure pressure surge.

vis.alt: Close view of a pilocarpine drop leaving the bottle tip and falling toward an upturned eye with a constricting pupil.
vis.caption: Pilocarpine drop being instilled into the eye, producing miosis through muscarinic stimulation. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Tertiary amine natural alkaloid cholinomimetics with superior tissue penetrance are exemplified by **pilocarpine**. Extracted from Pilocarpus microphyllus leaves, pilocarpine crosses corneal barriers to cause pupillary sphincter contraction, producing therapeutic miosis and opening trabecular outflow angles in acute closed-angle glaucoma. A related oral agent, cevimeline, acts on M3 receptors to stimulate saliva production in patients suffering from Sjogren syndrome xerostomia.
steps.say: Pilocarpine induces miosis to treat glaucoma, while cevimeline stimulates salivary flow in Sjogren syndrome.

steps.tx: Irreversible inhibition of cholinergic synaptic transmission can be produced by bacterial exoneurotoxins such as **botulinum toxin**. Secreted by Clostridium botulinum, the toxin light chain acts as an endopeptidase that cleaves presynaptic SNARE proteins, abolishing exocytotic fusion of acetylcholine vesicles at motor endplates. This produces flaccid paralysis used therapeutically for blepharospasm, cervical dystonia, spasticity, and axillary hyperhidrosis.
steps.say: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins to prevent acetylcholine release, producing flaccid muscle paralysis.
